```{r setup}
library(lpsugar)
library(ROI.plugin.highs)
```

This vignette focuses on different regression techniques that can be solved
using linear models.

$$
y_i = \sum_{j=1}^k{\beta_j x_{ij}} + e_i
$$
We start by generating the data we'll use.

```{r}
set.seed(123)
n <- 50
k <- 3

true_beta <- c(2, 3, -5)

x <- rpois(n*k, 6) |> matrix(n, k)
y <- x %*% true_beta + rnorm(n)
```


```{r echo=FALSE}
data.frame(x1 = x[,1], x2 = x[,2], x3 = x[,3], y = y) |> 
    head(5) |> 
    print.data.frame(row.names = FALSE)
cat("... and", n-5, "more rows")
```

## Least Absolute Deviation

The objective of Least Absolute Deviation (LAD) regression is to minimize the absolute
residuals $e_i$.

$$
\min{\sum_{i=1}^n{e_i}}
$$

Then the problem can be written like this:

$$
\begin{array}{rl}
  \min_{\beta,e} & \sum_{i=1}^n{e_i} \\
  \text{st} & e_i \ge |y_i - \hat{y_i}| \\
  \text{where} & \hat{y_i} = \sum_{j=1}^k{\beta_j x_{ij}}
\end{array}
$$

Believe it or not, the constraint is linear, despite containing an absolute value. 
`lpsugar` will simply expand the constraint into two. Together, they're equivalent
to the absolute value constraint.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& +e_i \ge y_i - \hat{y_i} \\
& -e_i \le y_i - \hat{y_i}
\end{aligned}
$$

Let's write the problem in `lpsugar`.

```{r}
n <- nrow(x)
k <- ncol(x)

lad <- lp_problem() |> 
    lp_var(beta[1:k]) |> 
    lp_var(e[1:n], lower = 0) |> 
    lp_min(sum(e)) |> 
    lp_alias(yhat = x %*% beta) |> 
    lp_con(e >= abs(y - yhat)) |> 
    lp_solve(solver = "highs")
```

The estimated $\hat{\beta}$ is quite similar to the `true_beta` $\beta$.

```{r}
cbind(
    true_beta = true_beta,
    lad_beta = lad$variables$beta |> round(2)
)
```

And the absolute deviation is:

```{r}
lad$objective
```


## Support Vector Machines

Support Vector Machines (SVM) are a binary classification method, that uses a hyperplane
to separate the groups.

$$
\begin{array}{rl}
x_{ij} \in \mathbb{R} &\quad i \in [1,n],\ j\in [1,k] \\
y_i \in \{\text{TRUE},\ \text{FALSE}\} &\quad i \in [1,n]
\end{array}
$$

Usually, $y$ is represented as $y_i \in \{-1, +1\}$, but I believe it's easier to understand
as a boolean variable.

### Basic Idea

An SVM finds a vector $\{w_j\}_{j\in[1,k]}$ and scalar $b$ that represents a hyperplane:

$$
\sum_{j=1}^k{w_j X_j} + b = 0
$$

Classifications works like this. If the *signed distance* from $x_{ij}$ to the hyperplane 
is positive, $y_i$ is predicted `TRUE`. If it's negative, $y_i$ is preficted `FALSE`.

$$
d_i = \sum_{j=1}^k{w_{j} x_{ij}} + b
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
d_i > 0  & \Rightarrow  y_i=\text{TRUE} \\
d_i < 0  & \Rightarrow  y_i=\text{FALSE}
\end{aligned}
$$

With this randomly generated data, we can find a line (which is an $\mathbb{R}^2$ hyperplane) that perfectly separates orange from blue.

```{r echo=FALSE}
set.seed(101)
n <- 20
k <- 2

true_w <- c(-3, +4)
true_b <- -2

x <- rnorm(n*k, mean = 5, sd = 3) |> 
    round(2) |> 
    matrix(n, k)

y <- x %*% true_w + true_b > 0

plot_svm <- function(x, y) {
    par(mai = c(0.9, 0.8, 0.2, 0.4))
    plot(x, col = ifelse(y, "royalblue", "orangered"), pch = 16)
}

plot_svm(x, y)
abline(a = 0, b = 0.75)
```

However, this is not the *best* separator. There are two methods of finding a better one,
a Hard Margin SVM and a Soft Margin SVM.

### Hard Margin

The goal of an SVM is to find the greatest possible *margin*. The margin is the smallest distance
from a point to the hyperplane. Minimizing the margin is equivalent to minimizing the quadratic sum of $w$ coefficients.

$$
\min_w \sum_{j=1}^k{w_j^2}
$$

And these constraints ensure the prediction is always correct.

$$
\begin{array}{rl}
d_i \ge +1  &\quad \forall i : y_i = \text{TRUE} \\
d_i \le -1  &\quad \forall i : y_i = \text{FALSE}
\end{array}
$$

The Hard Margin SVM can be written in `lpsugar` with the following code. 
The problem has a quadratic objective function and linear constraints.

```{r}
svm_hard <- lp_problem() |> 
    lp_var(w[1:k]) |> 
    lp_var(b) |> 
    lp_min(sum(w^2)) |> 
    lp_alias_manual(
        signed_dist[1:n],
        for (i in 1:n) signed_dist[i] = sum_over(w[j] * x[i,j], j = 1:k) + b
    ) |> 
    lp_con(
        for (i in which(y))  signed_dist[i] >= +1,
        for (i in which(!y)) signed_dist[i] <= -1
    ) |> 
    lp_solve(solver = "highs")
```

This is the result. The continuous line represent the hyperplane, and the dashed lines
represent the points where the hyperplane formula is $+1$ and $-1$.

```{r echo=FALSE}
plot_svm(x, y)

with(svm_hard$variables, {
     abline(a = - b / w[2], b = - w[1] / w[2])
     abline(a = (+1 - b) / w[2], b = - w[1] / w[2], lty = 2)
     abline(a = (-1 - b) / w[2], b = - w[1] / w[2], lty = 2)
})
```

### Soft Margin

Soft Margin SVMs allow some prediction errors. This means they support data that
cannot be linearly separated. A Hard Margin SVM would fail to find a feasible
solution with this data.

```{r echo=FALSE}
y[2] <- FALSE
y[3] <- FALSE
y[10] <- FALSE
plot_svm(x, y)
```

We will introduce a slack variable $\xi_i \ge 0$ indicating the prediction error for
observation $i$. Naturally, we want to minimize the prediction error, so we will update
the objective function:

$$
\min_w \sum_{j=1}^k{w_j^2} + C\sum_{i=1}^n{\xi_i}
$$

Where $C$ is known as the Regularization Hyperparameter.

The constraints will now allow some flexibility by adding the slack variables $\xi$:

$$
\begin{array}{rl}
d_i \ge +1 - \xi_i  &\quad \forall i : y_i = \text{TRUE} \\
d_i \le -1 + \xi_i  &\quad \forall i : y_i = \text{FALSE}
\end{array}
$$

In `lpsugar`, the Soft Margin SVM can be coded as follows.

```{r}
C <- 5 # Regularization Hyperparameter

svm_soft <- lp_problem() |> 
    lp_var(w[1:k]) |> 
    lp_var(b) |> 
    lp_var(slack[1:n], lower = 0) |> 
    lp_min(sum(w^2) + C * sum(slack)) |> 
    lp_alias_manual(
        signed_dist[1:n],
        for (i in 1:n) signed_dist[i] = sum_over(w[j] * x[i,j], j = 1:k) + b
    ) |> 
    lp_con(
        for (i in which(y))  signed_dist[i] >= +1 - slack[i],
        for (i in which(!y)) signed_dist[i] <= -1 + slack[i]
    ) |> 
    lp_solve(solver = "highs")
```

Notice that all blue values fall on top of the hyperplane, but some orange values
are incorrectly predicted.

```{r echo=FALSE}
plot_svm(x, y)

with(svm_soft$variables, {
     abline(a = - b / w[2], b = - w[1] / w[2])
     abline(a = (+1 - b) / w[2], b = - w[1] / w[2], lty = 2)
     abline(a = (-1 - b) / w[2], b = - w[1] / w[2], lty = 2)
})
```
